content: Root canal therapy is a series of procedures that involve cleaning, shaping, decontaminating, and filling the root canal system. Typically, this is performed through a hole drilled into the crown of the tooth, a process known as orthograde root canal therapy. However, when this approach fails, retrograde filling, which involves sealing the root canal from the root apex, serves as an alternative treatment option. Various materials are used for retrograde filling, but none fully meet the criteria for an ideal material. Therefore, selecting the most effective material is critical. This review updates a Cochrane Review initially published in 2016. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of different retrograde filling materials in children and adults requiring this procedure to preserve their teeth. The search for relevant studies was conducted across five bibliographic databases up to April 21, 2021, with additional searches in four Chinese-language databases. Both published and unpublished studies were considered. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing different retrograde filling materials were included, provided they reported success rates assessed through clinical or radiological methods with a minimum follow-up period of 12 months. The review process involved independent screening of records by two reviewers, who also independently extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Missing information was sought by contacting the original trial authors. Statistical analyses followed Cochrane guidelines, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Eight studies, all with a high risk of bias, were included in the review. These studies involved 1,399 participants and 1,471 teeth, and they were published between 1995 and 2019. Six comparisons of retrograde filling materials were analyzed: 1. Mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) vs. intermediate restorative material (IRM): The evidence suggests that MTA may have little to no effect on the success rate compared to IRM at one year. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low (risk ratio [RR] 1.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.97 to 1.22; I² = 0%; 2 studies; 222 teeth). 2. MTA vs. super ethoxybenzoic acid (Super-EBA): The evidence indicates that MTA may have little to no effect on the success rate compared to Super-EBA at one year, but the certainty of this evidence is very low (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.10; 1 study; 192 teeth). 3. Super-EBA vs. IRM: The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of Super-EBA compared to IRM on the success rate at one year. Results suggest that Super-EBA may either reduce or have no effect on the success rate (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.01; 1 study; 194 teeth). 4. Dentine-bonded resin composite vs. glass ionomer cement: Compared to glass ionomer cement, dentine-bonded resin composite may increase the success rate of treatment at one year. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low (RR 2.39, 95% CI 1.60 to 3.59; 1 study; 122 teeth). A similar result was observed when analyzing the root as the unit of analysis (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.09; 1 study; 127 roots). 5. Glass ionomer cement vs. amalgam: The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of glass ionomer cement compared to amalgam on the success rate at one year. Results suggest that glass ionomer cement may either reduce or have no effect on the success rate (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.12; 1 study; 105 teeth). 6. MTA vs. root repair material (RRM): The evidence suggests that MTA may have little to no effect on the success rate compared to RRM at one year. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.07; I² = 0%; 2 studies; 278 teeth). None of the included studies assessed adverse events associated with the materials. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine the superiority of any one retrograde filling material over another in root canal therapy. High-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to provide more definitive evidence.
